title: A Music Box: “Marcelle Cahn”—Prelude and Fugue No.8, Book II
content_blocks: Prelude and Fugue No.8 was inspired first by the preparations in the piano.  Carefully positioned brass screws between a single pair of strings for notes in the tenor through soprano registers, along with copper alligator clips on the wound strings in the bass created a “twangy” sound a little like a really sad music box.  I then devised a new mode to heighten that sense of sadness, which I call the “HyperAeolian” mode. In the way that it highlights (and repeats) the “sad” tones of the minor mode even more than the minor mode does, it somehow strikes me as “more sad than sad,” but in which the sadness becomes unmoored.

The pieces depict that unmoored sadness, responding to paintings by the French painter Marcelle Cahn (1895-1981): Femme et Voilier (Woman and Sailboat, 1927), and 4 Sphères (1960). Marcelle Cahn was a French painter of Jewish ancestry who studied literature, art, and philosophy in Germany, France, and Switzerland, and throughout her life skillfully straddled the line between figurative and abstract painting.

Even in the figurative Woman and Sailboat there is an abstraction of shapes and a flattening of space, yet it strikes me somehow as melancholy. This is reflected in the simple but directional shapes and lines in the prelude that nevertheless convey a depth of sadness.

Cahn’s later 4 Sphères is flatter and more abstract, comprising purely geometric shapes and recalls Kandinsky’s “constructivist” paintings (curiously, the spheres in the painting are actual three-dimensional balls); the fugue is similarly abstract and “constructed.” Yet even here there is what I perceive to be a loneliness in the image.

Mika Sasaki perfectly captured the sad tenderness of the Prelude, and the constructive-yet-lonely quality in the Fugue. These links are to newly-created videos of Mika’s recording session back in May, 2023—take a look!
